parts.note: a standard is a banner or flag carried in front of troops
a Pole is a person from Poland, a European

explanation.surface: A query about the regulation-issue staff used across Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard European' reads as one idea, a common continental type, but it splits into a banner and a nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: A staff can be the pole on which a flag is hoisted.

explanation.surface: Someone walking without shoes is told their efforts are futile.
explanation.definitionFit: Old-fashioned 'bootless' means futile or unavailing; read literally it means having no footwear on.

clue.text: Artist's turning as supporter of despot

indicators.note: turning signals that the letters of the word before are being rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A painter switches sides and backs a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' sounds like a change of allegiance; it is the anagram signal for the seven letters of 'Artist's' (the apostrophe adds nothing).
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was an absolute Russian ruler, so a backer of that autocratic regime is a royalist of this kind.

clue.text: These days, currency conversion is slow

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, marks the present era of dates
agio is the charge or premium paid when exchanging one currency for another

explanation.surface: A complaint that changing money nowadays takes ages.
explanation.walkthrough: AGIO is a banking term for the fee on exchanging money; crossword setters use it often.
explanation.definitionFit: Adagio is the musical tempo marking meaning at an unhurried, leisurely pace.

parts.note: the mountain in Turkey where, in Genesis, Noah's ark came to rest after the flood waters fell

explanation.surface: The tall summit that emerged after the Flood.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis says the ark grounded on the mountains of this name once the deluge subsided.

clue.text: Not fit, thought to be rash

parts.note: someone not fit is unwell, ill
thought, as in judged or deemed, means considered

explanation.surface: Someone unwell is judged to be reckless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rash' tempts as a skin complaint going with 'Not fit'; it is the definition, meaning hasty.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash decision is one made without proper thought, hasty and unwise.

explanation.surface: A mimic who does a famous French painter.
explanation.definitionFit: An entertainer doing impressions of celebrities has this title; Claude Monet led the 19th-century French art movement of the same name.

parts.note: twin, as in a matching pair, means double
keeping accounts with a bank is banking

explanation.surface: Two bank accounts opened by someone who parks badly.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage, double-banking means parking alongside a car already parked at the kerb, i.e. double parking.
explanation.definitionFit: Stopping a vehicle beside another already parked, blocking the road, is the inconsiderate practice this term names.

indicators.note: around tells us the drunkard's word is wrapped about the next piece

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
the Berkshire is a breed of pig, hence 'say' marking an example

explanation.surface: A tippler is found loafing somewhere in the English county of Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkshire looks like the English county; here it is a black breed of pig.
explanation.definitionFit: A spigot is a small wooden plug or tap stopping the vent of a cask.

clue.text: Severe outfit trimmed with gold, love us!

parts.note: a rig, or rig-out, is a set of clothes
or is the heraldic word for gold
love is nil in tennis, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone in a harsh gold-trimmed costume demands affection.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is gold in heraldry and O is love (a zero score in tennis).
explanation.definitionFit: Rigorous means strict and exacting, harsh in demands.

indicators.note: from shows the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A flower wreath handed over by friendly Pacific islanders.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark nods to Hawaii, where these flower garlands are given in welcome.
explanation.definitionFit: A lei is a Hawaiian wreath of flowers worn round the neck.

explanation.surface: Advice to slip into a different set of clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn into something new is one sense; to look good on someone, as a dress flatters its wearer, is the other.

parts.note: pictures workers chatting about their business when off duty, as though it were a meeting

explanation.surface: A business meeting held once the working day is over.
explanation.definitionFit: Discussion of work matters in social time, away from the job, is called this.

indicators.note: replacement suggests the letters of the word before are moved into new positions

explanation.surface: An elderly person getting a new hip joint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old character' looks like an elderly eccentric; it is a letter of the ancient Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Phi is the 21st letter of the Greek alphabet, an ancient script.

parts.note: 'as per' means in accordance with
SE, south-east, is the region of England round London where the home counties lie

explanation.surface: Gossip is said to come from the area around London.
explanation.walkthrough: The home counties are the English counties surrounding London, in the south-east (SE).
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse is to cast damaging, false aspersions on someone's reputation.

explanation.surface: Someone poking fun at an elderly spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To rib is to mock playfully; and in Genesis Eve, the first wife, was made from Adam's rib.

parts.note: M1 in Roman numerals is 1001, pointing to the Arabian Nights tales, whose woodcutter hero opens a cave with 'Open sesame'

explanation.surface: The first person mentioned in reports about Britain's main motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 looks like the London-to-Leeds motorway; read as Roman numerals M and I it is the Thousand and One Nights.
explanation.definitionFit: The woodcutter of the Arabian Nights story gets into the robbers' cave by saying 'Open sesame'.

clue.text: Striking on Sunday in large amounts

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the first piece sits on top of the next, so it comes before it

parts.note: striking, as with a whip, is lashing

explanation.surface: Workers walk out on Sunday in great numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' suggests an industrial walkout; it means hitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Lashings is informal British for plenty, as in heaps of cream.

parts.note: a round is one shot of ammunition, a bullet
in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: A newspaper delivery route that is well liked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'News-round' reads as a paper round; split it, 'News' defines and 'round' is ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulletin is a short broadcast or printed report of the latest events.

clue.text: These German pounds had no brass in them

definitions.text: These German pounds had no brass in them

parts.words: These German pounds had no brass in them
parts.note: pounds as enclosures, not money; brass is slang for officers, so these wartime German camps held other ranks rather than officers

explanation.surface: German currency that contained no copper alloy.
explanation.walkthrough: Pounds and brass suggest money; pounds are pens and brass is senior officers. In WWII officers went to separate Oflags.
explanation.definitionFit: These were WWII German prisoner-of-war camps for non-commissioned prisoners, while officers had their own.

clue.text: Vessel for cooling car, in the air

annotationWithheld.clue: Vessel for cooling car, in the air

parts.note: a sponsor at a christening stands as spiritual guardian to the baptised male child

explanation.surface: A lad backed by a charitable donor.
explanation.definitionFit: At baptism a godparent acts as sponsor, promising to oversee the child's faith.

clue.text: One who speaks of Job being ten short?

indicators.note: short means the work's title is missing the following element

parts.note: Job is a choral work for soloists and orchestra by Hubert Parry, on the Bible story
ten written as figures is 1 and 0, read as the letters IO

explanation.surface: A speaker talking about the biblical Job's suffering when ten is missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Job looks like the patient biblical figure; it is Parry's sacred choral piece. 'Ten' as 10 gives IO.
explanation.definitionFit: An orator is a public speaker, especially an eloquent one.

parts.note: such, as in to such a degree, means so
having great length is being long

explanation.surface: A query about a farewell speech that runs on far too far.
explanation.definitionFit: A casual phrase used on parting, meaning goodbye.

explanation.surface: Something left behind by a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The powder left when something burns is one sense; a common deciduous tree of the olive family is the other.

parts.note: bird is British slang for a prison sentence, from rhyming slang 'birdlime' for time
to pay a call is to visit

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at visiting someone in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coo!' looks like a British exclamation of surprise; it is the sound a pigeon makes. 'Bird' is British slang for a jail term.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigeon's soft cooing is the cry it makes, an example of an avian vocal sound.

clue.text: Wrath not entirely commendable, promoting peace

parts.note: ire is anger or wrath

indicators.note: not entirely means the word is left incomplete, its final letter dropped

parts.note: nice, meaning pleasant or good, stands for commendable

explanation.surface: Anger that is only partly praiseworthy is being used to keep the peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' cuts the last letter E from NICE, leaving NIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Irenic means conciliatory, aiming at reconciliation, from the Greek word for harmony.

clue.text: Complete, yet uneven condition at Ascot?

parts.note: tho, short for though, means yet or however
rough means bumpy or uneven
the going is the state of the turf at a racecourse such as Ascot

explanation.surface: A racegoer remarks that the ground at Ascot is bumpy.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a famous English racecourse; 'going' is racing jargon for the ground's condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Thoroughgoing means total, out-and-out, in every respect.
